overview: This file traces the tightening of Japanese foreign-exchange and capital controls in the Kwantung Leased Territory from late 1935 through 1938. It begins with a consular account of the territory’s mixed currency system—Bank of Chosen yen notes, Yokohama Specie Bank silver notes, and debased Chinese silver coin—and plans to withdraw the latter. Later despatches describe the October 1937 exchange-control regime as an effort to integrate the territory financially with Japan and Manchukuo, restrict imports, exports, travel funds, securities, loans, dividends, and capital movements, and displace foreign commercial interests. Internal State Department memoranda assess these reports, while three substantial translated enclosures reproduce the original 1937 ordinance, a supplementary import-payment order, and the extensive March 1938 amendments granting the Japanese Ambassador broad supervisory and discretionary powers.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Grummon on Kwantung currency and the 1935 exchange-control amendment
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports how the November 30, 1935 amendment to the foreign-exchange-control law might affect currency circulation in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: Grummon describes three currencies in local circulation: Bank of Chosen yen notes, Yokohama Specie Bank silver-yen notes, and small Chinese silver coins known as hsiaoyang-chien. He estimates that approximately nineteen million yen in notes circulated, divided between fifteen million in so-called gold notes and four million in silver notes. Authorities were considering withdrawing the small silver coin by March 1936, although banks and trade bodies favored delay, while the continued attachment of Chinese residents to silver was expected to sustain demand for silver notes.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Ballantine’s report on Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 64
subfiles.from: Department of State filing staff, referencing Joseph W. Ballantine at Mukden
subfiles.about: Directs the reader to another decimal-file location for Ballantine’s report and translations of Kwantung exchange-control legislation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers researchers to file 893.5151 Manchuria/7 for a December 12, 1935 communication from Mukden. That document contained translations of Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 64 of November 30, 1935 and the earlier Kwantung Government Order No. 44 of September 27, 1933.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum assessing the October 1937 Dairen despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, initialed JMJ
subfiles.about: Evaluates whether Grummon’s October 18 report on the Kwantung exchange-control law added significant new information.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the Manchukuo exchange-control law expressly applied to Manchuria, including the Kwantung Leased Territory. Because despatches from Mukden and Tokyo had already covered the subject thoroughly, the reviewer concluded that the Dairen report contained nothing new worth noting.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Grummon on the October 1937 foreign-exchange law
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the new law controlling foreign exchange, capital exports, imports, exports, travel funds, and foreign business in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: Grummon describes the October 8 law as an attempt to unify the Kwantung Leased Territory financially with Japan and Manchuria and to restrict foreign exchange leaving Japanese-controlled areas. The measure subjected trade to licensing, sharply limited exchange for firms and travelers, controlled securities, deposits, loans, dividends, and letters of credit, and anticipated prohibitions on luxury imports and preferences for Japanese goods. Foreign firms expected severe losses, and Grummon warned that discretionary enforcement could transfer importing and produce-exporting activity permanently into Japanese hands. He regarded the law as a major step toward eliminating the former free-trade zone and undermining the Open Door in Manchuria.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Dairen despatch No. 21
subfiles.from: Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the translated exchange-control ordinances transmitted from Dairen and comments on their discriminatory character.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum records receipt of translations of the October 1937 Kwantung exchange-control ordinance and its October 1937 and March 1938 amendments. Although Turner emphasized the Ambassador’s new discretionary power to favor Japanese banks and firms, the reviewer considered this relatively unimportant because the original decrees already openly favored Japan and exempted transactions involving Japanese yen.

subfiles.title: Turner’s despatch transmitting Kwantung exchange-control legislation
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits translations of the principal 1937 Kwantung exchange-control measures and their March 1938 amendment.
subfiles.summary: Turner encloses Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 12 of March 29, 1938, Foreign Exchange Control Ordinance No. 95, and Ordinance No. 97, both dated October 8, 1937. He explains that the earlier ordinances apparently had not previously been sent to the Department. Turner characterizes the March amendments as an effort to bring residents’ financial resources under closer official control and highlights provisions allowing the Japanese Ambassador to favor Japanese institutions and exercise wide, arbitrary authority.

subfiles.title: Translation of Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 12 of March 29, 1938
subfiles.to: Enclosed with William T. Turner’s despatch to the U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Amends the Kwantung foreign-exchange regulations to extend controls over foreign assets, loans, guarantees, property, reporting, and compulsory disposal.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance restricts foreign-currency loans, guarantees, bonds, overseas property, shipping, mining rights, investments, deposits, and other credits, while substantially expanding mandatory reporting. It reduces one reporting threshold from one thousand to one hundred yen and requires disclosures concerning overseas businesses, income, assets, liabilities, and capital movements. The Ambassador receives authority to grant exemptions, demand additional reports, inspect books, and order the sale or other disposition of gold, exchange, credits, and overseas property. Transactions governed by corresponding controls in Japan, Korea, Formosa, Karafuto, or Manchukuo are exempted from specified provisions.

subfiles.title: Translation of Foreign Exchange Control Ordinance No. 95
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau; enforced by Kenkichi Ueda
subfiles.to: Enclosed with William T. Turner’s despatch to the U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sets out the principal foreign-exchange-control regime for Kwantung Province and the South Manchuria Railway Zone.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance regulates exports of gold, purchases and sales of foreign currency, overseas remittances, securities, deposits, loans, trusts, insurance, letters of credit, and foreign-currency bond issues. It requires exporters to document drafts and repatriate proceeds, while prescribing extensive reporting by residents, securities dealers, banks, and exchange shops. Designated foreign-exchange banks receive limited operational exemptions but must verify customers’ permits and submit frequent transaction and position reports. Broad inspection, reporting, disposal, and penal powers are vested in the Ambassador, while transactions with Japan, Korea, Formosa, Karafuto, and Manchukuo receive preferential treatment or exemption.

subfiles.title: Translation of Kwantung Bureau Ordinance No. 97 on import payments
subfiles.to: Enclosed with William T. Turner’s despatch to the U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Imposes special controls on payments for imports, imports lacking foreign-exchange cover, and payments by foreign-exchange banks on outside instructions.
subfiles.summary: The order generally requires the Ambassador’s permission for foreign-exchange settlements and letters of credit connected with imports from outside Japan and Manchukuo, subject to monetary and transitional exceptions. It also controls the use of overseas securities, deposits, loans, and uncovered export proceeds to finance imports, and restricts imports not covered by foreign exchange. Banks must verify permits, major importers must report their historical payment settlements, and importers must submit permits and monthly reports through customs or the post office. The surviving text ends at the beginning of Article 15.

interest: The file is especially useful because it juxtaposes a detailed account of everyday monetary pluralism in Dairen’s hinterland with the comprehensive exchange-control machinery imposed only two years later. The translated ordinances expose the practical instruments of Japanese economic integration—licenses, exemptions, reporting requirements, inspections, forced asset disposal, and privileged treatment of transactions with Japan and Manchukuo—while the consular despatches record their expected impact on foreign firms and the Open Door. The internal memoranda also reveal differing State Department perspectives: consular officers emphasized discretionary discrimination and commercial displacement, whereas Washington reviewers sometimes regarded such discrimination as already explicit and therefore unremarkable. The June 22, 1938 review postdates the nominal closing date in the file title, and the final enclosure ends mid-article, both useful reminders of how the archival bundle was assembled.
